Pittsburgh Electric Propulsion
University of Pittsburgh
1. Background Research
For the PEP25 competition, our main goals were to keep the boat stable and fast. To lead
our research into hull design, we followed High Performance Marine Vehicles by Liang Yun and
Alan Bliault. The book goes through the different hull designs, their advantages and
disadvantages. Based on advantages and disadvantages presented in the paper, our team chose to
design a trimaran hull. The trimaran hull design presents an optimal balance of speed and
stability, making it an ideal candidate for the unmanned competition portion of PEP25. The
unique hull geometry minimizes hydrodynamic drag, increasing energy efficiency and extending
battery life – which is critical for electric propulsion. Furthermore, the enhanced stability of the
trimaran configuration improves operational safety. This innovative approach aligns with the
growing demand for sustainable marine solutions, positioning it as a competitive and
market-viable design.
Regarding control systems, after much initial research, it was decided to base the
autonomy stack on the popular robotics framework ROS2 Humble due to its node architecture
with various forms of internodal data streams allowing for easy communication between
differing sections of the autonomy and controls stack. Likewise, initial research regarding the
desired hardware, in consideration with the project’s budget, was done, involving searching for
an onboard computer, microcontrollers, and sensors.
2. Design & Analysis
2.1 Propulsion System & Hull Design
A brushless DC motor was selected as the type of motor for the boat. It offers high
efficiency along with precise control. After viewing many different companies, Electric
Motorsport was chosen. Their ME 1117 motor operates in the 48V range and runs at 6 hp, which
is well within the range our electrical system is designed for. Below is the motor curve for the
ME 1117 with our operating point highlighted.The motor offers a solid rotational speed, 3000 rpm, fit for a propeller and substantial

torque that works well within our operating conditions. No gear box will be required for this
motor. A picture of the motor is shown below.For our hull design, our team took inspiration from the USS Independence, an aircraft

carrier that was a trimaran hull with a larger central hull and smaller side amas for added
stability. Since our main goal for PEP25 is to achieve the fastest time, we decided to modify the
central hull to be a planing hull such that we could achieve the fastest times. For the design of the
central hull, our team took inspiration from a hydroplane called “Rocket”, which was designed
by William D. Jackson. “Rocket” was a common hydroplane for many boating enthusiasts as it
was relatively fast and inexpensive to manufacture.
To lead our propeller design, we followed The Propeller Handbook by Dave Gerr. The
book goes through all important steps and considerations to design a propeller. The key design
choices that were advised by this book were propeller type, number of blades, propeller diameter,
and propeller pitch. For propeller type, we chose a fixed-pitch propeller as they were common in
boats our size. A 3-blade propeller was also strongly recommended for boats in our size range, so
we decided to go with that. There are equations used for diameter and pitch in the book, which
we followed and are shown below.

From these specifications, we were able to design our propeller. The pitch allowed us to

3.1 Power Storage & Powertrain
The power storage system will be made up of two separate batteries, an off the shelf 12V
battery and a custom 48V battery. The 12V battery powers all low voltage systems, including the
autonomous hardware, servo motor, battery management system, and low voltage side of the
motor controller. The 48V battery powers only the boat’s powertrain.The 48V motor is built in a 13s5p configuration using Molicel P45B Li-ion cells. Based

on the values from the datasheet, we calculated a typical run time of 36 minutes and a run time of
12 minutes assuming the motor runs at top speed for the entire run. Estimates of motor power
were taken from the motor dynamometer curve above and calculations for run time are shown
below.

In terms of propulsion, the boat will feature an inboard. An inboard allows for a very
compact internal design, though it typically sacrifices some efficiency as the propeller is unable
to be completely horizontal with the water. Our design features a pair of universal joints that
allow the propeller to find that horizontal position, making an inboard extremely favorable to the
boat. Shown below is an isolated view of the inboard.
To support the inboard, there are two bearings. A shaft bearing is mounted along the
angled shaft to provide radial support. There is also a thrust bearing at the lower, propeller shaft.The thrust bearing provides all axial support necessary for the boat to function. The motor is

mounted to a custom motor mount and secured to the boat with screws. With this design, all
portions of the shafts are completely supported to limit any inefficiency in the power
transmission.
Other powertrain components, including the battery and motor controller, will be securely
mounted with screws inside the boat. Given the boat is 3D Printed, we were able to fully
integrate the mounting holes using heat set inserts, which are pressed in with a soldering iron and
have the filament melt around it. The components were strategically placed to minimize wire
length and simplify routing. The battery was placed inside of our electrical enclosure, which
includes, the BMS, LV battery, and contactor along with it.
For cooling, there are two components that must be considered: the battery and motor. To
determine the requirements of the system for the battery, we can look at its specifications. As
previously mentioned, we are using Molicel P45B cells, which have an internal resistance of 15
mΩ. At most, the battery will pull 100 amps of current in total, which splits up to 20 amps per
cell, given we are running in a 5-parallel configuration. Thus, the heat generated per cell is,

* . 015 = 6 𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑠
In total, the pack will generate,
𝑄𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑘 = 65 * 𝑄𝑐𝑒𝑙𝑙 = 65 * 6 = 390 𝑊𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑠
This is a very low overall heat. With supporting simulation data from Batemo, which we
unfortunately cannot share, the cell temperature will only increase by 10ºC without cooling.
Even assuming a very high outside temperature of 40ºC (104ºF), the battery temperature should
stay within the safe operating temperature of the cells, which have a maximum operating
temperature of 60ºC. Thus, cooling is not necessary for the battery pack.
For the motor, there are integrated cooling fans in the design. For this reason, we also do
not have to consider cooling system design for the motor.
3.2 Controls & Propulsion
To fabricate the propulsion system, we relied on mainly off-the-shelf components and
campus resources. The universal joints, angled shaft, and motor were purchased directly. The
motor mount, propeller shaft, and propeller were all manufactured and machined in-house. The
motor mount was manufactured by OshCut, a company based on Utah. The propeller shaft was
purchased online and machined down by SCPI, an on-campus machine shop. The propeller was
resin 3D printed by OpenLab, an on-campus makerspace.
Controlling the boat’s propulsion and rudder has been split into three primary
components that compose the entire autonomy stack. The perception software is responsible forestablishing and maintaining a constant stream of data from the boat’s sensors, ensuring the boat

has an accurate idea of its location relative to its initial point and the two buoys. This also
includes an object detection model to notify the boat of upcoming buoys. This information is
then sent to the path-planning code, which determines the next location of the boat. To get to the
next state of the boat, the controls stack interfaces with the motor and rudder, physically moving
the boat.
4. Risk Identification & Mitigation
Our club started the academic year facing serious financial constraints and a lack of
funding from our university, limiting our resources and design capabilities. Our financial account
previously started on a fiscal year basis, with funds depleting at the end of each school year.
Additionally, the same university organization that funded our club decided to cut our desired
budget and grant us only half of what we needed. The design process was able to continue;
however, using student-sponsored licenses, such as Orca3D, SolidWorks, and Ansys simulation
products. Although the fall semester was manageable, the upcoming build process for the
competition loomed on us, as our budget was far below what was needed to compete.
After months of communication and persuasion between university departments and
corporate connections, our business lead was able to land the club adequate funding from several
different sources. Not only was our club now funded, but different sources prevented the club
from being virtually bankrupt the next academic year because portions of the funds would roll
over. This came just in time, as the build process began almost immediately upon receiving
money. Purchases have been occurring frequently and supporting our sub-teams with the
products they need to build respective parts is a vital aspect of management of the club.
The main electrical risks are overcurrent, battery faults, and a breakdown of isolation
from either a short circuit or water intrusion. These risks are each mitigated using multiple parts
of the system, providing a level of redundancy.
Battery output current is constantly monitored by the BMS and motor phase current is
monitored by the motor controller. Both of these devices have programmed current limits, so if
the current measured exceeds that limit, they will shut down the battery or motor respectively.
The motor controller directly cuts power to the motor while the BMS controls a contactor on the
battery positive terminal which can disconnect the battery in the event of a fault. Should either of
these fail or if there is a sudden short, then a 150A fuse on the positive terminal of the battery
will blow, protecting the rest of the circuit and preventing a potential fire.
The condition of the 48V is constantly monitored by the BMS including by checking
individual cell voltages, total pack voltage, pack output current, and pack temperature. Each of
these characteristics have set limits based on our design calculations and on the datasheet for the
Molicel P45B. If these limits are exceeded, the BMS will act accordingly. In the event of most
safety critical faults, such as overcurrent or overtemperature, it will respond by opening the
contactor on the positive terminal of the battery, cutting it off from the rest of the circuit.Isolation between the 48V system and the rest of the boat is critical to ensuring proper

functionality of the boat’s systems. All of the electrical components on the boat are insulated and
kept as water-resistant as possible. If this insulation fails, the BMS has a built-in isolation
monitor which checks the electrical resistance between the battery terminals and the low voltage
ground. If this resistance falls below the programmed value, the BMS will assume that the
insulation between the 48V system and the rest of the boat has somehow failed, either due to
water intrusion or contact between a component on the 48V system and the rest of the boat. Most
metallic components on the boat that are not part of the electrical system are connected to the
low voltage ground (excluding some fasteners). This means that the BMS can detect whenever
any large metallic components are accidentally energized by the 48V system, so it can shut down
the battery.
The entire boat is 3D Printed with a mix of PLA and PETG filaments with about 5%
infill. Though this is quite weak, it doesn’t matter because the inside of the boat is primarily
serving as a mold. The goal of 3D printing is to easily integrate mounting holes and the inboard
into the boat. The entire structural integrity of the boat comes from the fiberglass added to the
outside of the hull. Several layers were added to increase strength and smooth the outside of the
boat, reducing drag. Because fiberglass is not waterproof, layers of glass reinforced body filler,
or bondo, were added to the outside. The combination of the bondo and fiberglass not only
ensures the boat will be strong enough in the water, but also that it can perform well in a marine
environment. On top of the bondo, layers of automotive paint were added. This makes the boat
look a lot nicer, along with smoothing the outside more, so it can perform better in the water.
There are three other points in the boat that require waterproofing, and we have different
solutions for each. For the lid, we have a gasket running around the entire outside that is
compressed when the lid is bolted into place. At the back of the boat, the rudder rod has an open
hole, which is covered with a tapered bellow. This allows the rod to easily move while also being
covered. The propeller shaft also has an open hole where it leaves the boat, which is covered
with shaft seal. Thus the entire boat is waterproof.
The only other mechanical risks would be mechanical failure of the propeller and
mechanical failure of the rudder, which undergo the largest forces of any component on the boat.
As previously mentioned, the propeller is resin printed, which should be strong enough to face
the water. The rudder is made of aluminum, so it should also have no problem in the water. The
pieces mounting the rudder will also undergo significant bending stress, so they are made with
aluminum and resin.
Due to the complexity and workload of developing an autonomous boat software stack,
the entire system was divided into four primary subteams (perception, path-planning, controls,
and simulation), with work then divided amongst individual members. To limit communication
failures that would later harm the integration of the entire autonomy stack, frequent architecture
discussions were held between the members of each subteam. This, in addition to frequently
creating visual representations of the software system and how each member’s contribution
would integrate with the others, was addressed early on before posing a larger problem.In terms of bugs and issues in the actual software itself, iterative unit and integration

testing was employed to ensure each module of the autonomy stack functioned as intended
individually and in combination with the others. Gazebo, a popular industry choice for robotics
simulation, was utilized to ensure our perception and path-planning worked as intended, with
real-time monitoring and data-logging using the visualizer Rviz2 confirming that the boat was
functioning correctly.
The primary risk regarding the autonomy stack was sensor failure. Each stream of data,
including GPS, IMU, and the manual RC controller receiver, has a form of data verification that
ensures the received serial data streams are not corrupted. Likewise, there are safeguards set in
place to ensure that the boat automatically shuts off when it fails to receive the information
necessary to operate safely. For instance, if the boat fails to receive GPS and RC controller data
streams for a set duration of time, the boat will act as if an emergency stop button was pressed.

ensures the boat will be strong enough in the water, but also that it can perform well in a marine
environment. On top of the bondo, layers of automotive paint were added. This makes the boat
look a lot nicer, along with smoothing the outside more, so it can perform better in the water.
There are three other points in the boat that require waterproofing, and we have different
solutions for each. For the lid, we have a gasket running around the entire outside that is
compressed when the lid is bolted into place. At the back of the boat, the rudder rod has an open
hole, which is covered with a tapered bellow. This allows the rod to easily move while also being
covered. The propeller shaft also has an open hole where it leaves the boat, which is covered
with shaft seal. Thus the entire boat is waterproof.
The only other mechanical risks would be mechanical failure of the propeller and
mechanical failure of the rudder, which undergo the largest forces of any component on the boat.
As previously mentioned, the propeller is resin printed, which should be strong enough to face
the water. The rudder is made of aluminum, so it should also have no problem in the water. The
pieces mounting the rudder will also undergo significant bending stress, so they are made with
aluminum and resin.
Due to the complexity and workload of developing an autonomous boat software stack,
the entire system was divided into four primary subteams (perception, path-planning, controls,
and simulation), with work then divided amongst individual members. To limit communication
failures that would later harm the integration of the entire autonomy stack, frequent architecture
discussions were held between the members of each subteam. This, in addition to frequently
creating visual representations of the software system and how each member’s contribution
would integrate with the others, was addressed early on before posing a larger problem.In terms of bugs and issues in the actual software itself, iterative unit and integration
testing was employed to ensure each module of the autonomy stack functioned as intended
individually and in combination with the others. Gazebo, a popular industry choice for robotics
simulation, was utilized to ensure our perception and path-planning worked as intended, with
real-time monitoring and data-logging using the visualizer Rviz2 confirming that the boat was
functioning correctly.
The primary risk regarding the autonomy stack was sensor failure. Each stream of data,
including GPS, IMU, and the manual RC controller receiver, has a form of data verification that
ensures the received serial data streams are not corrupted. Likewise, there are safeguards set in
place to ensure that the boat automatically shuts off when it fails to receive the information
necessary to operate safely. For instance, if the boat fails to receive GPS and RC controller data
streams for a set duration of time, the boat will act as if an emergency stop button was pressed.
